description: We are a passionate group of developers and creators dedicated to blending education with technology. Space-themed STEM content is often either too basic or overly complex for youth. We want to bridge that gap by building a gamified mission simulator that makes high-stakes aerospace engineering trade-offs intuitive, tangible, and highly addictive for the next generation of space explorers.
summary: HORIZON 710 is a browser game for students aged 11-13 that turns real space-mission trade-offs into play, answering the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players choose a crew of 4 from 5 specialists and pack a 150-unit shuttle (radiation shield, power supply, life support), watch a launch sequence, then survive four Sols (Mars days) in a 3D base. Each Sol is inspired by NASA missions and research: dust on solar panels (InSight), food and a greenhouse (ISS Veggie), a global dust storm (Opportunity), and a solar flare (DONKI-style alert). Every choice costs power, life support or crew health, and early choices come back later. It matters because students learn that engineering is about trade-offs, not single right answers.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
HORIZON 710 is a decision-based game for students aged 11-13. The player follows one mission from the launch pad to Mars. Before launch, a guide named Pip helps the player choose a crew of 4 from 5 specialists (Commander, Engineer, Scientist, Medic, Communications Officer) and pack a shuttle under a strict 150-unit cargo limit: radiation shield (Hydrogen Polymer: 30 units, 100% protection on Sol 4; Hydrogen BNNT: 10 units, 80%), power supply (nuclear battery RTG: 30 units, steady 3 power; lightweight battery: 10 units, drops to 2 on Sol 4 because of the cold) and life support (1 cargo unit per life support unit, max 100). After a launch sequence and an approach to Mars, the crew lives four Sols in an explorable 3D base.

HOW IT WORKS
The right astronaut must do each job, and every action costs power, life support or crew health. The HUD tracks all three. Each night the base uses 20 life support.

Sol 1, Dust: the Engineer or Commander cleans the solar panels within 30 seconds (inspired by NASA’s InSight lander).

Sol 2, Food: packaged food degrades. Only the Commander can build the greenhouse, which uses power but later makes life support and protects health (inspired by ISS Veggie).

Sol 3, Dust storm: contact Ground Control, then cover the panel, return the rover and send the crew inside. Each choice changes the penalties on Sol 4 (inspired by the 2018 storm that ended the Opportunity rover).

Sol 4, Solar flare: a DONKI-style alert. The Commander activates shelter support and sends everyone inside within 30 seconds. The shield chosen before launch decides the damage.
Poor decisions can hurt right away or become delayed faults. The game ends with a 1-3 star Mission Report, then the player can retry or roam freely. Each Sol has a “More Info” pop-up that tells the real NASA story in kid-friendly words.

BENEFITS
Students feel why engineers trade weight, power and safety, and learn real NASA mission history while playing. It needs no install, works on desktop and phones, and shows all guidance as text.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE
A classroom-ready trainer. Next steps: a Moon route with cold lunar nights, a playable GO/NO-GO Launch Director stage, Bangla language, teacher reports, and live NASA DONKI data.

TOOLS
One HTML file: JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Three.js r128 (3D scene and effects), Web Audio (sound effects), Google Fonts. Textures, models and sounds are generated by our own code.

AI DISCLOSURE
Code generated with AI assistance (Claude Code); prompts refined with Gemini; demo narration generated with ElevenLabs.

STATUS
First prototype. The Moon is shown but not yet playable, and the launch is a guided sequence. Source code: https://github.com/usernaxaoa/HORIZON-710
